plan.topic: Planning a pregnancy on semaglutide or tirzepatide: what the labels, the new international consensus and a Sept 2026 meta-analysis say
plan.angle: 'Planning a Pregnancy on Semaglutide or Tirzepatide? Questions to Bring to Your Prescriber'. Slide 2: 'Weight loss may affect fertility, and some early studies in PCOS suggest changes in ovulation. Early evidence, not a fertility treatment.' Use a confirmed source or drop the claim. Slide 3: '10 observational studies: no clearly detectable increase in [outcomes listed], but authors say this does not establish safety or support use in pregnancy.' Slide 4: verbatim label line plus revision date, framed as 'label guidance to review with your prescriber'. Slide 5: verbatim tirzepatide contraception line plus revision date, plus 'ask your prescriber which method fits you'. Slide 6: the Lancet OGWH consensus, labelled 'in women with type 1, type 2 or gestational diabetes'. Slide 7: prescriber/OB-GYN questions, including 'If I become pregnant unexpectedly, who do I call first?' and 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own; call your prescriber.' Slide 8: the prescriber line. No 'Ozempic babies', no emoji hook.
plan.working_title: Planning a Pregnancy on Semaglutide or Tirzepatide? What Labels and New Evidence Say
plan.why: Rising topic with fresh primary sources (meta-analysis, consensus, JCEM) that matters to the women 25–45 in our audience. A checklist people will want to save, and the topic hasn't been covered in 30 days. | fact-check: Topic is allowed and useful, but sensitive. Verified: the 'no clearly detectable increase' meta-analysis is a systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 observational studies in 2,118,215 women (8,325 exposed within 6 months before a positive pregnancy test). The authors explicitly say the findings 'do not establish safety or support continued use during pregnancy' and 'may offer limited reassurance'. That limit must appear on the same slide. Note the EMJ write-up lists the journal as 'Medicine'. Confirm journal, date (Sept 2026?) and DOI from the paper itself, and cite the paper, not EMJ. International consensus verified: Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women's Health 2026, 'Preconception, pregnancy, and postnatal use of GLP-1 receptor agonist-based therapies in women with type 1, type 2, or gestational diabetes…'. Its population is women WITH DIABETES. It must not be presented as guidance for people using GLP-1s for weight without diabetes. NOT verified: a 'JCEM 2026' PCOS fertility paper. The only 2026 item I found was a JBRA Assisted Reproduction narrative review. The writer must locate and confirm the JCEM paper or drop slide 2's citation. Labels: quote the current Wegovy/Ozempic PI wording ('discontinue … at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy') with the revision date, credited as label text. Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) oral-contraceptive note: quote the label verbatim with the revision date. Don't paraphrase it into dose-escalation instructions. Packaging: avoid 'fertility boost' framing and anything that implies GLP-1s as a fertility treatment (off-label). Analytics note for the owner: carousels reach 0–3 accounts. Consider rebuilding as a Short later, but that isn't a safety issue.

package.title: Planning a Pregnancy on Semaglutide or Tirzepatide? Questions to Bring to Your Prescriber

social.instagram_caption:
Planning a pregnancy while on semaglutide or tirzepatide? Here's what the US labels say, so you can plan it with your prescriber.

Semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy): half-life ~1 week. The Ozempic label says to stop at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy "due to the long washout period"; the Wegovy label gives the same 2-month timing for weight or heart-risk use.

Tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound): half-life ~5 days. No set stop-ahead window — the Zepbound label says stop when pregnancy is recognized. The labels also note tirzepatide may reduce how well oral birth control pills work, with a non-oral or added barrier method advised for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase.

For both medicines, the labels say human pregnancy data are too limited to establish or evaluate risk.

Save this for your next appointment and bring the questions in slide 6 to your prescriber and OB-GYN. Share it with someone who's planning ahead.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation. Don't stop or change your medicines on your own — talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary: I checked every label claim against the current US prescribing information, and all four labels support the content. Ozempic (Revised 5/2026, read on DailyMed) gives a half-life of about 1 week and says the drug is "present in the circulation for about 5 weeks after the last dose". Its quote "Discontinue OZEMPIC in women at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy due to the long washout period for semaglutide" is word for word. It describes human data as limited and says animal studies show possible risk to the fetus. Wegovy (Revised 6/2026) covers both the injection and the tablets. It has the 2-month stop "because of the long half-life of semaglutide", says human data are "insufficient to establish" risk, and includes "Weight loss offers no benefit to a pregnant patient and may cause fetal harm." Mounjaro (Revised 8/2026) gives a half-life of about 5 days, says pregnancy data are "insufficient to evaluate" risk and sets no stop-before-pregnancy window. It also has the oral contraceptive advice and says the stomach-emptying delay is "largest after the first dose". Zepbound (Revised 8/2026) gives a half-life of "approximately 5-6 days", has the same "weight loss offers no benefit" line and contraceptive advice, and says to stop when pregnancy is recognized. The safety framing is good: it says not to stop or change medicines on your own, flags diabetes management, brings in the OB-GYN, includes the prescriber line and gives no dosing. Four small wording fixes are listed below.

issues.claim: Mounjaro label text: "Advise females using oral hormonal contraceptives to switch to a non-oral contraceptive method or add a barrier method of contraception for 4 weeks after initiation and for 4 weeks after each dose escalation."
issues.problem: The wording inside the quote marks may not match the Mounjaro label exactly. In the current label text I retrieved, it begins "Advise patients using…", and the Zepbound version has a comma and adds "with ZEPBOUND". Only the label's exact printed words belong inside quote marks. The meaning itself is accurate.
issues.fix: Replace the body with: "The Mounjaro and Zepbound labels advise people using oral hormonal contraceptives to switch to a non-oral method, or add a barrier method, for 4 weeks after starting and for 4 weeks after each dose increase."

issues.claim: The Wegovy label also says to stop at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy, citing semaglutide's long half-life.
issues.problem: This drops part of the label's scope. Wegovy's 2-month line applies to people taking it for CV risk reduction or weight reduction, and for MASH only "where the potential risk outweighs the potential benefit".
issues.fix: Replace the second sentence with: "The Wegovy label also says to stop at least 2 months before a planned pregnancy (for weight or heart-risk use; for MASH, when the risk outweighs the benefit), citing semaglutide's long half-life."

issues.problem: This is accurate, but on its own it could read as "you can keep taking it into pregnancy". The Zepbound label says to discontinue when pregnancy is recognized, and weight loss offers no benefit in pregnancy.
issues.fix: Change the value to: "No set window; Zepbound label: stop when pregnancy is recognized"

issues.claim: Plan pregnancy with your prescriber; don't stop or change medicines on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.
issues.problem: The body has the prescriber line but no general educational disclaimer.
issues.fix: Replace the body with: "Plan pregnancy with your prescriber; don't stop or change medicines on your own. Educational only, not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you."
